chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 101 to 120: short speeches of the love situation in every land. Men weigh earth and heaven against one day of embrace, or find a strong man undone by a slip of a girl; women burn whether they remember or try not to, curse the cock that ends a night beside the husband, hang between love and the town's talk, and face evenings and north winds that bring no one; the friend fixes trysts, mocks the mother's diviner and turns slipping bangles into a jibe.

101.reading: The man says that the sea-girt world and the hard-won land of the gods, weighed together, are not worth the day he lies arm in arm with the young girl whose kohl eyes are like flowers and whose body is like gold.
101.nuance: தூக்கின் is the language of the balance: he does not say heaven is bad, only that both worlds on one pan do not lift a single day (வைகல்) of embrace on the other.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is the joy of union itself; no native thing is named

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; he states it as his own verdict

102.reading: The woman says that if she thinks of him her heart burns, and not thinking is beyond her strength; this love has grown till it touches the sky, and the man she has clung to is not one of the noble.
102.nuance: The bind is closed on both sides (உள்ளின் ... உள்ளாது இருப்பின்), and the last line turns from her pain to a judgment on him: சான்றோர் அல்லர், not noble, because he lets a love this large burn her.

thinai_evidence.note: lament in absence, with no native thing to place it

103.reading: The woman tells her friend that in the shivering mire gathered by the flood, where even the red-beaked egret hunting its food is pained by the spray the cold north wind drives, he seems not to be coming, and she seems not to be going to live.
103.nuance: The two lines end alike (வாரார் போல்வர் / வாழேன் போல்வல்): his not coming and her not living are set as matching guesses. The egret, which only suffers and does no act of the lovers, sets the mood and is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the egret in the flood-mire of the shore

104.reading: The woman tells her friend that her lover left in the dew season, when cold drops fall like pearls from a broken string and the cool thaali creeper is grazed at dawn, and the days of parting will be many.
104.nuance: The season is the cruelty: he left not in summer but in the cold, when the pearl-like dew and early grazing mark each morning she counts alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the man has gone away; the things are of the cold pasture

105.reading: The woman says that the bond with the man of the dread hill, where a peacock that unknowingly ate the rich millet ears set aside for the god trembles in the heat like a possessed dancing woman, has become something she remembers with streaming eyes.
105.nuance: The peacock's fault is innocent (அறியாது உண்ட): it took what belonged to the god of the hill and now shakes like one seized. Her own wasting would be read at home as the god's seizure, and the hill is named சூர், the dreadful.

thinai_evidence.note: hill millet, the peacock and the hill god

ullurai.tenor: the girl who took the hill man's love

pairs.situation: she took his love without knowing what it would cost
what she took belonged to the dread hill and its man, not freely hers
she now burns and trembles, eyes streaming

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses a peacock and millet of her own hill field, things she knows (porul 7.26)

106.reading: The woman tells her friend that word has come from the man of the land where the white roots of the itti, climbing the rock, look like a waterfall coming down the slope, spoken from a heart without guile, and they should take it up as fire takes ghee and send back word that they are as good as wedded to him.
106.nuance: தான் மணந்தனையம் claims the standing of a wife while love is still secret; the eager fire of ghee is hers, the friend is drawn into the reply (நாமும்).

thinai_evidence.note: the fig on the rock and the hill waterfall

comparisons.tenor: the itti's white roots on the rock
how eagerly they should receive his word

107.reading: The wife curses the cock with its crest like a cluster of thondri flowers: may it fall prey to the young wildcat that watches for house rats at midnight and come to cruel harm, for it woke her from the safe sweet sleep she slept beside the lord of the rich, well-watered town.
107.nuance: The curse is elaborate and patient (the cat that waits at midnight for rats), which measures how sweet the broken sleep was; ஏம இன் துயில், safe sweet sleep, is the sleep of a wife at home, and the cock's crow is the dawn that ends it.

thinai_evidence.note: the lord of the rich watered town, and dawn

108.reading: The woman tells her friend that in the little village under the hill where rain clouds play, as the milch cows head back to their calves, the bright jasmine of the green-leaved scrub has taken on the beauty of the red sky, and she thinks she will not survive.
108.nuance: The poem never says 'evening' or 'he has not come': the cows turning to their calves and the jasmine opening red in the sunset do it for her, and the last line is the whole of her speech.

thinai_evidence.note: scrub forest, rain and the red evening

iraicchi.act: the milch cows go back to their calves at dusk
iraicchi.sense: even the cattle return to their young at nightfall, but her man has not come back to her

109.reading: The friend says of the lord of the shore, where the waves bring in a great swarm of thorny-legged, bent-backed prawns, that even in the days when the two were together the beauty of the girl's fine forehead was not as it is now.
109.nuance: மன்னோ marks something past and gone: her forehead was lovely then, and is pale now; said in the third person, it is a reproach meant for the man's hearing. The prawns that the waves bring are only the shore's plenty here; reading them as a hidden picture fails the two-pair test.

thinai_evidence.note: prawns cast up by the sea at the lord's shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she speaks of both lovers in the third person; no addressee is named

110.reading: The woman asks her friend what he is to them now, come or not, the man who never asked what had become of her in the cold cruel north wind that ruffles the blue water-lilies, sways the karuvilai spotted like peacock feathers and scatters the soft flowers of the thorny eengai.
110.nuance: Her dismissal (யாராகியரோ, who is he to us) is the measure of her hurt; what she holds against him is not absence but the question he never asked (என்னாயினள்கொல்).

thinai_evidence.note: bush flowers of the scrub under the wind

comparisons.tenor: the bright spots of the karuvilai flower

111.reading: The friend says that if the mother too takes the diviner's word that victorious Neduvel caused the sickness that has loosened the girl's soft arms, then let the man of the hill, where dark boulders look like a stub-tailed cow elephant with its trunk tucked in, come quickly, so they may see the household's great foolishness laughed at.
111.nuance: The friend wants the man's arrival to expose the rite: the household will be the joke (பெருநகை) once its god-sickness turns out to be love. சிறிதே at the end keeps the mockery mild.

thinai_evidence.note: the diviner of Murugan and the hill man

comparisons.tenor: the dark crowded boulders of the hill

112.reading: The woman tells her friend that if she fears the town's talk her love will waste, and if she lets restraint go only shame is left; she is like the fibrous branch a great elephant has bent, broken but not fallen to the ground; see what he has done to her beauty.
112.nuance: The branch is held up by its own bark fibre (நாருடை): what keeps her from falling is the thread still joining her to him, which is also what the gossip would cut.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill elephant bending a branch; secret love under the town's talk

comparisons.tenor: the woman caught between love and shame

113.reading: The friend tells the man the place: the pond is near the town, the little forest stream not far from the pond, and the grove there is visited by nothing but the white heron looking for food; she and the friend will go there to fetch rich clay for their hair, and the great simpleton will come there too.
113.nuance: The directions are laid out as a chain (town, pond, stream, grove), and the heron is both the grove's only visitor and the sign that no one else will see. பெரும்பேதை, the great simpleton, is the friend's fond word for the girl who will come.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend fixes a secret tryst, the uri of kurinji, among things of the town's fields

114.reading: The friend tells the man of the well-made chariot that she has come to his trysting place leaving her doll lying in the neythal field, and asks leave to go, since every evening the egret, its belly full of aaral fish, tramples her little daughter's forehead.
114.nuance: The 'daughter' is the doll she has left on the shore, a playful pretext to leave the lovers alone; the reading of என்மகள் as the doll is ours and the joke depends on it.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flats, the egret and the aaral fish

115.reading: The friend tells the man of the good hill, where the soft-gaited wild cow sleeps on the cool fragrant slope, that even those who do great good may be slighted, but though she has only one good in her, he should be kind with a perfected love so that her sulking ends, for she has no one but him.
115.nuance: The wild cow sleeping unafraid on his slope stands for the safety she should have in his grace; the opening maxim is a warning turned gently against him.

thinai_evidence.note: the wild cow on the hill slope

iraicchi.act: the wild cow sleeps unafraid on the man's slope
iraicchi.sense: as the creatures of his hill rest secure there, the girl who has no one but him should rest secure in his kindness

116.reading: The man says that the honey-dripping hair of the woman he loves and lives with is like the fine sand drawn into ripples at the great ford of Uranthai of the rich Cholas, well parted, fragrant and cool.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the beloved in union; no native thing places it

117.reading: The friend says of the lord of the shore, where a wet crab, frightened by the watch of the heron white as a rain-season lily, rushes to its hole among the mangrove roots like a herdsman's bull that has snapped its rope, that if he does not come, let it be: there are bangles here in the sellers' hands, small ones too.
117.nuance: The jibe is that her bangles slip as she wastes, so she will need smaller ones, and these can be bought: the friend makes light of his absence to sting him. Read as a hidden picture (the crab fleeing the heron's watch as the girl hiding from the town's eyes) it has two pairs, but the poem names no watch or gossip to anchor them, so it fails condition 4.

thinai_evidence.note: crab, mangrove and the lord of the shore

comparisons.tenor: the crab rushing to its hole

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the man is spoken of in the third person; the jibe reads as meant for his hearing

118.reading: The woman tells her friend that in the loveless evening that has come down thick, when birds and beasts settle in loneliness and those shutting the much-used gate call out whether anyone else is coming, her lover does not come.
118.nuance: The gatekeepers' call (வருவீர் உளீரோ) is the cruel detail: the house asks every evening who is still to come, and the one answer she waits for never comes.

thinai_evidence.note: lament at nightfall; the evening and the shut gate are all the setting

119.reading: The man says that as the striped young of a small white snake can strike down a forest elephant, so this young girl with teeth like sprouts and bangles on her hands has struck him down.
119.nuance: அணங்குதல் is what a god or demon does to a person; the scale of the simile (a hatchling snake, a wild elephant) is the hero's own wonder at being undone by someone so small and young.

thinai_evidence.note: the forest elephant of the hills

comparisons.vehicle: சிறுவெள் ளரவின் அவ்வரிக் குருளை கான யானை அணங்கி
comparisons.tenor: the young girl who has overpowered him

120.reading: The man tells his heart that it has longed for something hard to get, like a poor man longing for pleasure: it knew the beloved was good, but did not know she was hard to reach.
120.nuance: The two knowings are set against each other (நல்லள் ஆகுதல் அறிந்து / அரியள் ஆகுதல் அறியாது): the heart learned her worth and missed its price, which is where the simile of the poor man's wish bites.

thinai_evidence.note: the man in secret love finds her hard to meet; no native thing is named

links.note: Both have the man set the gods' world against lying in the beloved's arms: the Kural asks whether Vishnu's world is sweeter, Kuruntokai 101 puts earth and heaven together on one pan of a balance against a single day of embrace.
links.teaches: The Kural's open question about heaven has an older Sangam answer: the poet had already weighed both worlds together against one day and found them light, so the couplet's question reads as an allusion to that verdict rather than a doubt.

links.note: Both put the woman in the same bind, nearly in the same words (உள்ளின் உள்ளம் வேமே; உள்ளினும் உள்ளம் சுடும்): remembering burns her and not remembering is impossible.
links.teaches: The Kural keeps Avvaiyar's bind and drops her last line, the charge that the man is not noble, so set side by side they show the couplet turning a complaint against him into a pure description of her state.

links.note: In Akananuru 122 the house cock and the owl that eats house rats are among the night's watchers that keep the secret lover away; in Kuruntokai 107 the wife curses the cock for ending her sleep beside her husband and wishes it prey to the wildcat that hunts house rats.
links.teaches: Held together they show that marriage did not free the lovers' night from its old enemy: the cock that guarded the house against the secret lover still cuts short the wedded night, and the wife's curse sends it to the very rat-hunters of the courtship poem.

links.note: Both make the woman's pain open with the evening: the Kural's sickness buds at dawn and blooms at evening, and in Kuruntokai 108 the jasmine opens red in the sunset as the cows go home and she says she will not survive.
links.teaches: The Kural's flower metaphor for the sickness rests on a real mullai sight that Kuruntokai 108 shows, the jasmine opening at red dusk as the herds return, so the couplet's conceit is that scene folded into the body of the woman who watches it.

links.note: In Kuruntokai 111 the friend wishes the hill man would come and expose the household that believes the diviner's word about Murugan; in Akananuru 22 the girl, embraced by her lover on the very night of the rite, laughs (நக்கனென்) at the offering wasted on a stranger priest.
links.teaches: The laugh the friend in Kuruntokai 111 hopes for is the laugh the girl of Akananuru 22 actually has, so together they show the veriyattu rite was framed in akam as a comic error waiting for the lover's arrival to undo it.

links.note: Both hang the woman between love and shame: the Kural has the two hung from a carrying pole that is her life, Kuruntokai 112 names the town's talk as the fear and pictures her as a branch an elephant has snapped that still hangs by its fibre.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai 112 gives the Kural's evenly balanced pole a cause and a breaking point: the weight on shame's side is the town's gossip, and the balance is already a break held only by a strand, which the couplet's still image does not show.

links.note: Both tie the slipping bangles to the absence of the lord of the shore (துறைவன்): in the Kural they announce his leaving to the town; in Kuruntokai 117 the friend says let him stay away, smaller bangles can be bought from the sellers.
links.teaches: The same sign of wasting is grief in the woman's mouth and a weapon in the friend's: Kuruntokai 117 shows the slipping bangle could be turned into mockery meant to shame the man, which the Kural's lament never does.

links.note: In the Kural the woman pities the evening as a fellow sufferer and asks if its mate is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 118 the evening is loveless (நாரில்) and the birds and beasts that settle in loneliness are company she gets no comfort from.
links.teaches: Read together they show two answers to the same hour: the Kural's woman finds a companion in the grieving evening, while the Sangam woman finds the whole world, beasts and gatekeepers included, going home around her, so the evening isolates rather than consoles.

links.note: Both have the man say that his strength has been broken by a young girl: the Kural by her bright forehead alone, though foes in battle feared him; Kuruntokai 119 by the likeness of a hatchling snake felling a wild elephant.
links.teaches: Kuruntokai 119 supplies the image behind the Kural's paradox of the mighty man undone by a forehead: the elephant brought down by a hatchling snake, a picture of poison not strength, which explains why the couplet's warrior has no defence.

source_issues: 115: lines 3 and 4 (இலைகவர் பாடமை ஒழுகிய) are hard to construe; the slope's description is read only as cool and fragrant, and the verse is marked uncertain.
105: the repaired line 6 (the poet's name moved to `poet`) reads cleanly as the end of the poem.
